questions.stem: What is the key anatomical difference between BKA and AKA?

choices.text: The terms describe wound dressings rather than amputation levels
choices.explanation: They describe the level of lower-limb amputation.

choices.text: BKA preserves the knee; AKA removes the limb above the knee
choices.explanation: Knee preservation is the main functional distinction.

choices.text: Both remove the knee joint
choices.explanation: BKA preserves the knee.

choices.text: BKA is above the hip and AKA is below it
choices.explanation: This reverses and misstates the levels.

questions.point: BKA preserves the knee, whereas AKA is above the knee and generally requires more energy for mobility.

questions.stem: Which focused sequence is most appropriate after lower-limb amputation?

choices.text: Only phantom sensation
choices.explanation: Phantom pain matters but is not the entire assessment.

choices.text: Diet preference, sleep pattern, then wound appearance
choices.explanation: This omits immediate postoperative risks.

choices.text: Only prosthetic fit on the first postoperative assessment
choices.explanation: Early care prioritizes bleeding, wound, circulation and pain.

choices.text: Bleeding, wound/infection, residual-limb circulation, pain and position
choices.explanation: These are the high-yield postoperative nursing priorities taught.

questions.point: Post-amputation nursing assessment prioritizes bleeding, wound/infection, residual-limb circulation, pain and position.

questions.stem: How should phantom limb pain be understood?

choices.text: It is real pain perceived in the removed limb and should be assessed and treated
choices.explanation: Phantom pain is a recognized neurological phenomenon.

choices.text: It means the amputation level was documented incorrectly
choices.explanation: Phantom pain does not indicate a documentation error.

choices.text: It is always a sign of wound infection
choices.explanation: It can occur without infection.

choices.text: It proves the patient is imagining symptoms
choices.explanation: The pain is not dismissed as imagination.

questions.point: Phantom limb pain is real pain perceived in the removed limb.

questions.stem: Why should prolonged flexion of a residual limb be avoided?

choices.text: It increases blood production
choices.explanation: This is unrelated to positioning.

choices.text: It guarantees faster wound closure
choices.explanation: This is not the purpose of contracture prevention.

choices.text: It prevents all phantom pain
choices.explanation: Positioning does not guarantee prevention of phantom pain.

choices.text: It can contribute to flexion contracture and loss of range of motion
choices.explanation: Prolonged flexed positioning can shorten tissues and impair function.

questions.point: Avoid prolonged flexion because it can promote flexion contracture; follow the positioning and physiotherapy plan.

questions.stem: A post-amputation dressing becomes rapidly blood-soaked and the patient becomes tachycardic. What is the priority?

choices.text: Wait for the next scheduled dressing round
choices.explanation: Possible hemorrhage requires prompt action.

choices.text: Focus first on phantom pain education
choices.explanation: Bleeding takes priority.

choices.text: Assess circulation/vitals and escalate urgently for possible hemorrhage
choices.explanation: Rapid bleeding with tachycardia can indicate significant blood loss.

choices.text: Encourage independent walking before assessment
choices.explanation: Mobilization is unsafe before evaluating possible hemorrhage.

questions.point: Active or increasing bleeding after amputation requires urgent assessment and escalation.

questions.stem: Why should pain be reassessed as a trend rather than treated as a number alone?

choices.text: Unexpectedly worsening pain can signal a new limb complication
choices.explanation: Pain trend can reveal deterioration such as neurovascular compromise or infection.

choices.text: Only the first pain score is clinically useful
choices.explanation: Response and change over time matter.

choices.text: Pain severity always identifies the exact diagnosis
choices.explanation: Pain alone is not diagnostic.

choices.text: A lower score means neurovascular checks are unnecessary
choices.explanation: Other limb findings still matter.

questions.point: Unexpectedly worsening orthopaedic pain should trigger reassessment for a cause, not just repeated analgesia.

questions.stem: Which medication-safety pairing is correct?

choices.text: Gabapentin: it cannot contribute to drowsiness
choices.explanation: Gabapentin can cause drowsiness and ataxia.

choices.text: Tramadol: respiratory status never matters
choices.explanation: Sedation and respiratory depression can occur.

choices.text: Ketorolac: combine freely with other NSAIDs
choices.explanation: Duplicate NSAIDs increase adverse-effect risk.

choices.text: Paracetamol: count the total from all products
choices.explanation: Duplicate acetaminophen/paracetamol can create overdose risk.

questions.point: Common IBD2 analgesics require product-specific safety checks: total paracetamol, no duplicate NSAIDs, and sedation/respiratory monitoring for sedating drugs.

questions.stem: What should be checked after a sedating analgesic is given?

choices.text: Only the colour of the tablet package
choices.explanation: Packaging does not assess patient response.

choices.text: Only the wound dressing label
choices.explanation: This does not assess medication safety.

choices.text: Pain response, alertness and respiratory status
choices.explanation: These show both benefit and important adverse effects.

choices.text: Only the next scheduled dose time
choices.explanation: Reassessment must include clinical effect.

questions.point: After analgesia, reassess pain response and monitor alertness/respiration when sedating medicines are used.

questions.stem: A fracture patient reports severe pain that is much worse than expected and passive stretch increases it. What should come before simply giving more analgesia?

choices.text: Wait until the pain score reaches 10/10
choices.explanation: Urgency is not defined by one numerical threshold.

choices.text: Assume tolerance to pain medicine has developed
choices.explanation: This can miss limb-threatening deterioration.

choices.text: Encourage weight-bearing to test the limb
choices.explanation: This is unsafe in a potentially compromised limb.

choices.text: Repeat the neurovascular assessment and escalate concern
choices.explanation: The pain pattern can warn of acute compartment syndrome.

questions.point: Danger pain requires limb and neurovascular reassessment before assuming the problem is inadequate analgesia.

questions.stem: Why are exact routes, contraindications and interaction details kept in the Medication Library rather than memorized from this lesson?

choices.text: The trade name alone determines safe administration
choices.explanation: The exact generic, formulation and order must be verified.

choices.text: All analgesics share identical administration rules
choices.explanation: They do not.

choices.text: They are drug- and product-specific and must match the current order and reference
choices.explanation: Medication safety details change by product, formulation and patient context.

choices.text: They are unimportant to nursing care
choices.explanation: They are important but belong in the verified medication entry.

questions.point: Use the verified medication entry and current order for drug-specific administration, contraindications and interactions.

questions.stem: What should be verified before mobilizing an orthopaedic patient?

choices.text: The strength of the bed rails alone
choices.explanation: This does not determine weight-bearing status.

choices.text: Only whether the patient wants to walk
choices.explanation: Preference matters but does not replace safety orders.

choices.text: Weight-bearing status, assistive device and required staff help
choices.explanation: These determine whether and how mobilization is safe.

choices.text: Only the room number
choices.explanation: This does not establish mobility safety.

questions.point: Before mobilizing, verify prescribed weight-bearing status, assistive device and needed assistance.

questions.stem: Which areas deserve particular pressure-injury attention in an immobile patient?

choices.text: Sacrum and heels
choices.explanation: These are common pressure points in bedbound patients.

choices.text: Only the scalp
choices.explanation: This is not the main routine focus.

choices.text: Only the fingertips
choices.explanation: This misses major weight-bearing pressure areas.

choices.text: Only the wound incision
choices.explanation: Pressure risk exists beyond the surgical site.

questions.point: Immobility requires skin inspection and repositioning/weight shifts, especially at high-risk pressure areas such as sacrum and heels.

questions.stem: Which new limb pattern most strongly suggests DVT?

choices.text: Isolated shoulder stiffness
choices.explanation: This does not suggest lower-limb DVT.

choices.text: Symmetric cool feet without pain
choices.explanation: This does not fit the taught DVT pattern.

choices.text: Bilateral hand itching after soap
choices.explanation: This is unrelated.

choices.text: Unilateral swelling, pain, warmth and redness
choices.explanation: This is a classic concerning DVT pattern.

questions.point: New unilateral swelling, pain, warmth or redness should raise concern for DVT.

questions.stem: An immobilized patient suddenly develops dyspnea and chest pain. What is the priority?

choices.text: Massage the painful calf vigorously
choices.explanation: Manipulation is not an appropriate response to suspected DVT/PE.

choices.text: Wait for routine physiotherapy review
choices.explanation: This delays emergency assessment.

choices.text: Urgent escalation for possible pulmonary embolism while assessing ABCs/vitals
choices.explanation: PE is a medical emergency.

choices.text: Encourage unassisted walking to improve circulation
choices.explanation: This is unsafe during possible PE.

questions.point: Sudden dyspnea/chest pain in a VTE-risk patient requires emergency escalation for possible PE.

questions.stem: Which prevention approach best matches the taught VTE plan after fracture repair?

choices.text: Use compression even when specifically contraindicated
choices.explanation: Patient-specific orders and contraindications matter.

choices.text: Start anticoagulation independently without an order
choices.explanation: Anticoagulants require the authorized plan.

choices.text: Keep every patient on strict bed rest regardless of orders
choices.explanation: Unnecessary immobility increases complications.

choices.text: Mobilize when allowed and follow prescribed anticoagulation/compression
choices.explanation: These are established prevention measures when appropriate.

questions.point: VTE prevention may include early mobilization when allowed plus prescribed anticoagulation and compression.

questions.stem: What does an elevated CRP tell you by itself?

choices.text: The infecting organism is known
choices.explanation: A culture is needed to identify an organism.

choices.text: The patient must have a normal WBC count
choices.explanation: CRP does not determine the WBC result.

choices.text: Osteomyelitis is definitively diagnosed
choices.explanation: CRP alone cannot diagnose osteomyelitis.

choices.text: Inflammation is present, but the source is not identified
choices.explanation: CRP is nonspecific.

questions.point: CRP is a nonspecific inflammatory marker and must be interpreted with the clinical picture and trend.

questions.stem: Which CBC information is most useful in an infected orthopaedic patient?

choices.text: Only hemoglobin to identify the infecting organism
choices.explanation: Hemoglobin does not identify microorganisms.

choices.text: Only the platelet count for every clinical question
choices.explanation: Platelets do not replace WBC or hemoglobin assessment.

choices.text: WBC/neutrophils for infection context, hemoglobin for blood loss/anemia, and platelets for bleeding/clotting context
choices.explanation: Each component answers a different bedside question.

choices.text: Only the mean cell volume
choices.explanation: This misses the key infection, anemia and platelet information.

questions.point: CBC components support infection, anemia/blood-loss and bleeding-risk assessment.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a correctly collected culture?

choices.text: Identify an organism and help guide antimicrobial choice
choices.explanation: Culture can support targeted antimicrobial therapy.

choices.text: Determine weight-bearing status
choices.explanation: That comes from the orthopaedic plan.

choices.text: Replace wound assessment
choices.explanation: Culture results must be interpreted with the patient and wound.

choices.text: Measure the patient's pain severity
choices.explanation: Pain requires clinical assessment.

questions.point: A correctly collected culture helps identify the organism and guide antimicrobial therapy.

questions.stem: A patient with suspected fracture-related infection is unstable and septic. Cultures have not yet been collected. What is the safest principle?

choices.text: Ignore cultures permanently once treatment begins
choices.explanation: Sampling can still be important when clinically feasible.

choices.text: Withhold all treatment until every specimen is collected
choices.explanation: This can dangerously delay care.

choices.text: Do not delay urgent treatment solely to obtain cultures
choices.explanation: Sepsis requires immediate assessment and treatment.

choices.text: Use CRP alone to choose the antibiotic
choices.explanation: CRP does not identify the organism.

questions.point: In an unstable septic patient, urgent treatment must not be delayed solely for culture collection.

questions.stem: CRP and ESR remain elevated, but the wound and patient are clinically improving. What is the best interpretation?

choices.text: Use the trend with the clinical picture; the markers alone do not prove worsening osteomyelitis
choices.explanation: Inflammatory markers are supportive rather than diagnostic by themselves.

choices.text: The high markers prove treatment failure
choices.explanation: This overinterprets nonspecific tests.

choices.text: Stop all clinical assessments because labs are available
choices.explanation: Bedside findings remain essential.

choices.text: Assume the culture result is irrelevant
choices.explanation: Microbiology may remain important to treatment decisions.

questions.point: Inflammatory markers support assessment but do not diagnose or define worsening osteomyelitis by themselves.

choices.text: Action performed by the surgeon
choices.explanation: This is not the SBAR definition.

choices.text: Allergies only
choices.explanation: Allergies may be background information but do not define A.

choices.text: Admission date only
choices.explanation: This belongs in background if relevant.

questions.point: SBAR means Situation, Background, Assessment and Recommendation/Request.

questions.stem: Which documentation best supports continuity after a patient deteriorates?

choices.text: Patient bad
choices.explanation: This is vague and nonobjective.

choices.text: Time, objective findings, action, person notified, instructions and reassessment
choices.explanation: This records the event and response clearly.

choices.text: See previous note
choices.explanation: This does not document the current change.

choices.text: Doctor informed
choices.explanation: This omits what happened and what followed.

questions.point: Document time, objective findings, action, notification, instructions and the patient's response/reassessment.

questions.stem: Why is read-back used for new verbal or telephone orders?

choices.text: To let the nurse change the order wording
choices.explanation: The goal is confirmation, not alteration.

choices.text: To replace documentation entirely
choices.explanation: The communication still needs documentation.

choices.text: To avoid identifying the patient
choices.explanation: Patient identification remains essential.

choices.text: To confirm accuracy before carrying out and documenting the order
choices.explanation: Read-back reduces communication error.

questions.point: New verbal/telephone orders should be repeated back according to policy and documented.

questions.stem: A patient with an external fixator develops fever, worse pain and purulent drainage. Which SBAR opening is strongest?

choices.text: Background: the hospital opened many years ago
choices.explanation: This is irrelevant background.

choices.text: Situation: new fever, increased pain and purulent drainage in this patient now
choices.explanation: It immediately states the current problem.

choices.text: Assessment: the patient has a bed in the ward
choices.explanation: This does not describe the clinical change.

choices.text: Recommendation: no review is needed because a dressing is present
choices.explanation: The findings require review.

questions.point: A useful SBAR begins with the current change, then relevant background, focused assessment and a clear request.

questions.stem: Which note is weakest after escalating a neurovascular change?

choices.text: Timed neurovascular findings with the person notified and repeat assessment
choices.explanation: This supports continuity.

choices.text: Objective description of sensation and movement before and after escalation
choices.explanation: This documents the clinical trend.

choices.text: Recorded instructions received and patient response
choices.explanation: This completes the communication loop.

choices.text: “Doctor informed” with no time, findings or response
choices.explanation: This is insufficient for tracking what changed and what happened next.

questions.point: Avoid vague documentation such as “doctor informed” without the clinical details and follow-up.

choices.text: Assessment, with the immediate problem stated in Situation
choices.explanation: Assessment carries the findings; Situation states why you are calling.

choices.text: Recommendation only

choices.text: They should be omitted to keep the call short
choices.explanation: Concise communication still needs critical findings.

choices.text: Background only
choices.explanation: Background gives relevant history/context.

questions.stem: After reporting a new limb-safety problem, what should the chart show?

choices.text: Only the medication list

choices.text: Nothing until discharge
choices.explanation: Documentation should be timely.

choices.text: Only the words “team aware”
choices.explanation: This is too vague.

choices.text: Time, findings, action, notification, instructions and reassessment
choices.explanation: These document the clinical event and response.

questions.stem: A fracture patient has severe increasing pain on passive stretch and tingling, but a pulse is present. What is the priority?

choices.text: Give analgesia and end the assessment
choices.explanation: Pain relief must not replace emergency assessment.

choices.text: Encourage walking to test the limb
choices.explanation: This is unsafe.

choices.text: Urgent neurovascular reassessment and escalation for compartment syndrome
choices.explanation: A pulse does not exclude acute compartment syndrome.

choices.text: Wait until the pulse disappears
choices.explanation: Pulselessness is a late finding.

questions.point: Recognize compartment syndrome despite a palpable pulse and escalate urgently.

questions.stem: An external fixator has purulent drainage and a component appears loose. What should the nurse do?

choices.text: Ignore the drainage if the pulse is present
choices.explanation: A pulse does not exclude infection or hardware problems.

choices.text: Assess the patient/limb, protect it and escalate without adjusting the frame
choices.explanation: Both infection and mechanical problems require authorized review.

choices.text: Tighten the frame before checking the patient
choices.explanation: Independent adjustment can alter alignment.

choices.text: Allow unrestricted walking to test stability
choices.explanation: This is unsafe.

questions.point: External-fixator infection or hardware problems require assessment, protection and escalation without independent adjustment.

questions.stem: A post-BKA dressing rapidly soaks with blood and the heart rate rises. What is the priority?

choices.text: Focus on phantom pain first
choices.explanation: Hemorrhage takes priority.

choices.text: Wait for the next scheduled dressing change
choices.explanation: This delays urgent care.

choices.text: Begin routine gait training
choices.explanation: Mobility is not the immediate priority.

choices.text: Assess circulation/vitals and escalate for possible hemorrhage
choices.explanation: Bleeding with tachycardia is a postoperative emergency concern.

questions.point: Rapid postoperative bleeding after amputation requires urgent hemorrhage assessment and escalation.

questions.stem: An immobilized orthopaedic patient develops unilateral calf swelling, then sudden dyspnea and chest pain. What is the best response?

choices.text: Massage the calf and reassess tomorrow
choices.explanation: Massage is not appropriate and delay is unsafe.

choices.text: Ask the patient to walk unassisted
choices.explanation: This is unsafe.

choices.text: Treat as possible PE: assess ABCs/vitals and escalate urgently
choices.explanation: This is an emergency VTE pattern.

choices.text: Assume deconditioning explains the symptoms
choices.explanation: Sudden cardiopulmonary symptoms need emergency review.

questions.point: Possible DVT with sudden cardiopulmonary symptoms requires emergency escalation for PE.

questions.stem: A fracture patient's pain is much worse today despite analgesia. Which action best integrates the IBD2 approach?

choices.text: Reassess neurovascular status, wound/infection and hardware before assuming analgesia is inadequate
choices.explanation: Worsening pain may be the first sign of a complication.

choices.text: Use CRP alone to decide the cause
choices.explanation: A lab result cannot replace bedside assessment.

choices.text: Document the pain score and take no further action
choices.explanation: Trend and cause matter.

choices.text: Increase medication independently without reassessment
choices.explanation: This can mask deterioration and exceeds scope.

questions.point: Unexpected worsening pain requires reassessment for limb, wound and hardware complications.

questions.stem: CRP and ESR are high while the wound and patient are clinically improving. What is the correct interpretation?

choices.text: The high values prove worsening osteomyelitis
choices.explanation: This overinterprets nonspecific markers.

choices.text: The wound examination can now be stopped
choices.explanation: Clinical assessment remains necessary.

choices.text: Culture results no longer matter
choices.explanation: Microbiology can still guide treatment.

choices.text: The markers are nonspecific and must be interpreted with the clinical trend
choices.explanation: They support but do not define the diagnosis alone.

questions.point: Inflammatory markers do not replace the patient, wound and overall trend.
